sectionTitle: Waves in air, fluids and solids — part 4.6.1.2

specStatements.text: Students should be able to describe wave motion in terms of their amplitude, wavelength, frequency and period.
The amplitude of a wave is the maximum displacement of a point on a wave away from its undisturbed position.
The wavelength of a wave is the distance from a point on one wave to the equivalent point on the adjacent wave.
The frequency of a wave is the number of waves passing a point each second.
period = (1)/(frequency)
period, T, in seconds, s
frequency, f, in hertz, Hz
The wave speed is the speed at which the energy is transferred (or the wave moves) through the medium.
All waves obey the wave equation:
wave speed = frequency × wavelength
[v = f λ]
wave speed, v, in metres per second, m/s
frequency, f, in hertz, Hz
wavelength, λ, in metres, m
Students should be able to:
• identify amplitude and wavelength from given diagrams
• describe a method to measure the speed of sound waves in air
• describe a method to measure the speed of ripples on a water surface.
(Physics only) Students should be able to show how changes in velocity, frequency and wavelength, in transmission of sound waves from one medium to another, are inter-related.

Required practical activity 8: make observations to identify the suitability of apparatus to measure the frequency, wavelength and speed of waves in a ripple tank and waves in a solid and take appropriate measurements.
AT skills covered by this practical activity: AT 4.
This practical activity also provides opportunities to develop WS and MS. Details of all skills are given in Key opportunities for skills development.

scopeNotes.statement: AT skills covered by this practical activity: AT 4.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Required practical activity 8 is treated purely as a laboratory skills requirement, and the apparatus work is held to the single apparatus-and-techniques statement the specification names for it: making observations of waves in fluids and solids to identify the suitability of apparatus for measuring frequency, wavelength and speed, and taking those measurements. Everything the practical content asks a student to do — choosing between a ruler and a strobe image in a ripple tank, deciding whether a stopwatch can time a single ripple, reading a frequency from a signal generator, measuring across ten wavelengths — sits inside that one skill. No apparatus or technique from another AT statement (electrical measurement, measuring motion of objects, temperature, chemical apparatus) is introduced under this practical, and the numbered AT descriptors themselves are never set as recall: they describe what a student does at the bench, not content to be learned and examined.

scopeNotes.statement: This practical activity also provides opportunities to develop WS and MS. Details of all skills are given in Key opportunities for skills development.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The working scientifically and mathematical opportunities are exercised through the practical content rather than taught as a separate list. The mathematical skills used are exactly those the wave work requires — substituting into and rearranging v = f λ and T = 1/f, converting centimetres to metres and kilohertz to hertz, and dividing a distance across ten wavelengths by ten to obtain a mean. The working scientifically points are the ones the practical itself raises: reducing the effect of measurement uncertainty by measuring over many wavelengths or many echoes, repeating readings, and judging whether a piece of apparatus is precise enough for the quantity being measured. The WS and MS reference codes are not reproduced, taught or examined here as recallable content, because the specification names them as opportunities for skills development, not as subject content.

concepts.definition: Any wave, transverse or longitudinal, can be described using four quantities: its amplitude (how far points move from rest), its wavelength (how long one complete wave is), its frequency (how many waves pass a point each second) and its period (how long one complete wave takes to pass). Amplitude describes the size of the oscillation; wavelength, frequency and period describe its timing and spacing. Frequency and period are two ways of stating the same information, since T = 1/f.

The amplitude of a wave is the maximum displacement of a point on a wave away from its undisturbed position. It is measured from the undisturbed (rest) line to the top of a crest, or from the undisturbed line down to the bottom of a trough — it is not the distance from a crest all the way down to a trough, which is twice the amplitude. Amplitude is a distance and is measured in metres, m, on a displacement axis.

The position a point in the medium occupies before the wave arrives, and the position it returns to as the wave passes — the flat water level before a ripple reaches it, or the centre line on a wave diagram. Amplitude is always measured from this line, so on a diagram the undisturbed position must be identified before the amplitude can be read off.

The wavelength of a wave is the distance from a point on one wave to the equivalent point on the adjacent wave. In practice this means crest to the next crest, or trough to the next trough, or any point to the point one whole wave further on. For a longitudinal wave it is the distance from one compression to the next compression. Its symbol is the Greek letter lambda, λ, and wavelength, λ, is in metres, m.

The frequency of a wave is the number of waves passing a point each second. If 50 complete waves pass a fixed point every second the frequency is 50 Hz. Frequency is set by the source that makes the wave — the dipper in a ripple tank, the vibrating string, the loudspeaker cone — and it is not changed by the material the wave travels through.

The unit of frequency: frequency, f, in hertz, Hz. One hertz means one complete wave passing a point each second. Larger frequencies use prefixes — 1 kHz = 1000 Hz and 1 MHz = 1 000 000 Hz — and these must be converted to hertz before being used in the wave equation.

The period is the time taken for one complete wave to pass a point, and period, T, is in seconds, s. It is calculated from period = (1)/(frequency), written in symbols as [T = 1/f]. A wave of frequency 4 Hz has a period of 1/4 = 0.25 s; a wave of period 0.5 s has a frequency of 2 Hz. This equation is one of those provided on the AQA Physics equation sheet, so it does not have to be recalled, but it must be selected and applied correctly.

The wave speed is the speed at which the energy is transferred (or the wave moves) through the medium. Wave speed, v, is in metres per second, m/s. It is fixed mainly by the medium: sound travels at roughly 340 m/s in air, far faster in water and in solids, and every sound in a given room travels at the same speed whatever its pitch or loudness.

All waves obey the wave equation: wave speed = frequency × wavelength, written in symbols as [v = f λ]. It holds for every wave — sound in air, ripples on water, waves along a string, light — and for transverse and longitudinal waves alike. This is one of the equations students must be able to recall and apply; it is not given on the equation sheet. Rearranged it gives f = v ÷ λ and λ = v ÷ f.

In [v = f λ]: wave speed, v, in metres per second, m/s; frequency, f, in hertz, Hz; wavelength, λ, in metres, m. Data are often supplied in other units — a wavelength in centimetres, a frequency in kilohertz — and must be converted before substituting, or the answer will be wrong by a factor of 100 or 1000.

concepts.term: Reading amplitude and wavelength from a diagram
concepts.definition: On a transverse wave diagram, first find the undisturbed line; the amplitude is the distance from that line up to a crest (or down to a trough), and the wavelength is the distance from any point to the equivalent point on the adjacent wave, most easily crest to adjacent crest. Where the horizontal axis is distance, that measurement is a wavelength; where the horizontal axis is time, the same measurement gives the period instead. For a longitudinal wave drawn as compressions and rarefactions, the wavelength is measured from the centre of one compression to the centre of the next.

concepts.term: Measuring the speed of sound waves in air
concepts.definition: Two standard methods. (1) Two microphones a measured distance apart (for example 1.0 m, measured with a metre rule) are connected to a fast timer or an oscilloscope. A sharp sound is made beyond one microphone; the timer records the very short interval between the sound reaching the first and second microphone; speed = distance ÷ time, repeated and averaged. (2) The echo method: stand a measured distance from a large flat wall, clap, and time the echoes — timing many echoes and dividing reduces the effect of reaction time. The sound travels to the wall and back, so speed = (2 × distance) ÷ time for one echo. Either method gives a value of about 330–340 m/s.

concepts.term: Measuring the speed of ripples on a water surface
concepts.definition: Set up a ripple tank with a lamp above it so that the ripples cast shadows on white paper beneath. A dipper driven by a motor and signal generator produces straight ripples at a frequency read from the signal generator. Freeze the shadow pattern with a strobe light or a photograph, lay a rule alongside it, measure the length of ten wavelengths and divide by ten to obtain λ. The speed is then found from v = f λ. Alternatively, at a low frequency, time a single ripple crossing a measured distance with a stopwatch, giving speed = distance ÷ time, although this is less precise because the ripple is faint and the reaction time is large.

concepts.term: Required practical activity 8: waves in a ripple tank and in a solid
concepts.definition: The practical asks which apparatus is suitable for measuring frequency, wavelength and speed, and then requires those measurements to be taken. In a ripple tank the frequency is read from the signal generator driving the dipper (a stopwatch cannot resolve individual ripples), and the wavelength is measured across ten shadow wavelengths with a rule. For waves in a solid, a vibration generator is clamped to a stretched string held taut by a hanging mass over a pulley; the frequency is set and read from the signal generator, and the frequency is adjusted until the string vibrates in clear loops that appear to stand still. The length of one loop is half a wavelength, so measuring several loops with a metre rule gives λ, and the speed of the wave along the string is v = f λ.

concepts.term: Sound passing from one medium to another (Physics only)
concepts.definition: When a sound wave passes from one medium into another — air into water, air into a brick wall — the source is still producing the same number of waves each second, so the frequency does not change. The speed does change, because speed depends on the medium. Since v = f λ and f is fixed, the wavelength must change in the same proportion as the speed: λ = v ÷ f. Sound travels faster in water than in air, so its wavelength in water is longer; a wave entering a medium in which it travels more slowly has a shorter wavelength. Velocity, frequency and wavelength are inter-related in exactly this way.

concepts.term: Wave speed is not the speed of the particles
concepts.definition: The wave speed is the speed at which the energy is transferred through the medium, not the speed at which any part of the medium travels. As a sound wave crosses a room at about 340 m/s, each air particle only oscillates back and forth about its own undisturbed position; as a ripple crosses a tank, a floating cork bobs up and down but does not move to the far side.

misconceptions.question: On a wave diagram, what distance is the amplitude?
misconceptions.correct: The amplitude is the maximum displacement of a point away from its undisturbed position, measured from the undisturbed line to a crest (or to a trough).
misconceptions.misconception: The amplitude is the height of the wave from the bottom of a trough to the top of a crest.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The full crest-to-trough distance is the most visually obvious measurement on a wave diagram, and everyday language calls that 'the height of the wave'. The undisturbed line is often not drawn on the diagram, so students measure between the two features they can actually see.
misconceptions.correction: Find the undisturbed position first — the centre line the wave oscillates about — and measure from there. Crest to trough is twice the amplitude, so a wave whose crests are 3 cm above the line and troughs 3 cm below has an amplitude of 3 cm, not 6 cm.

misconceptions.question: Where does one wavelength start and end on a wave diagram?
misconceptions.correct: One wavelength is the distance from a point on one wave to the equivalent point on the adjacent wave, for example crest to adjacent crest.
misconceptions.misconception: One wavelength is the distance from a crest to the trough next to it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Crest and trough are the two features students learn to name, so the gap between them looks like a natural unit. The word 'wave' is also used loosely for the hump above the line, making the hump look like one whole wave.
misconceptions.correction: Crest to the neighbouring trough is only half a wavelength. The measurement must return to an equivalent point — going from a crest, past a trough, and up to the next crest. Measuring across ten of these and dividing by ten is the reliable way to do it.

misconceptions.question: What does the frequency of a wave tell you?
misconceptions.correct: The frequency is the number of waves passing a point each second.
misconceptions.misconception: The frequency tells you how fast the wave is travelling, so a high-frequency wave is a fast wave.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In everyday speech 'frequent' and 'fast' are close in meaning, and a high-frequency wave does look busier. Students also meet frequency and speed in the same equation without separating what each one counts.
misconceptions.correction: Frequency counts waves per second at a fixed point; speed measures how far the wave travels per second. In air, a 100 Hz note and a 4000 Hz note travel at the same speed — the high note simply has a shorter wavelength.

misconceptions.question: How are the period and the frequency of a wave related?
misconceptions.correct: period = (1)/(frequency), so T = 1/f, with period, T, in seconds, s and frequency, f, in hertz, Hz.
misconceptions.misconception: The period and the frequency are the same number, so a wave of frequency 40 Hz has a period of 40 s.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both quantities describe how often waves arrive, and both are taught in the same sentence. If the reciprocal in the equation is not noticed, the two are treated as interchangeable and the units get swapped as well.
misconceptions.correction: They are reciprocals, not equals. A high frequency means a short period: 40 Hz gives T = 1 ÷ 40 = 0.025 s. Frequency is measured in hertz, period in seconds, and the two units are never interchangeable.

misconceptions.question: In a given material, what happens to the frequency of a wave if its wavelength is longer?
misconceptions.correct: Because the speed is fixed by the medium, a longer wavelength means a lower frequency: fewer, longer waves pass each second.
misconceptions.misconception: A longer wavelength means more waves pass every second, because each wave covers more ground.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students reason that a bigger wave must deliver more, and they treat wavelength and frequency as two measures of the same 'size' rather than as quantities linked inversely through a fixed speed.
misconceptions.correction: Rearrange the wave equation: f = v ÷ λ. With v fixed, increasing λ decreases f. Long ocean swells arrive slowly and far apart; short ripples arrive rapidly.

misconceptions.question: When a sound wave travels across a room at 340 m/s, what is moving at 340 m/s?
misconceptions.correct: The wave itself — the disturbance and the energy it transfers — moves through the air at 340 m/s.
misconceptions.misconception: The air particles themselves travel across the room at 340 m/s, carrying the sound with them.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The wave clearly gets from the speaker to the listener, and the only thing between them is air, so students assume the air must have made the journey. The distinction between a travelling disturbance and travelling matter is genuinely hard.
misconceptions.correction: The wave speed is the speed at which the energy is transferred through the medium. Each air particle only oscillates about its own undisturbed position; the pattern of compressions moves on, the air does not.

misconceptions.question: Which waves does the equation v = f λ apply to?
misconceptions.correct: All waves obey the wave equation, transverse and longitudinal, in any medium and in a vacuum.
misconceptions.misconception: The wave equation only works for transverse waves, because you need a visible wavelength between crests to use it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Every diagram used to derive the equation is a transverse one with crests and troughs, so the equation gets attached to that picture rather than to the general idea of a repeating disturbance.
misconceptions.correction: A longitudinal wave has a wavelength too — the distance from one compression to the next. The specification states that all waves obey the wave equation, and it is used for sound just as readily as for ripples or light.

misconceptions.question: A sound wave passes from air into water. What happens to its frequency?
misconceptions.correct: The frequency is unchanged; the speed increases and so the wavelength increases in the same proportion.
misconceptions.misconception: The frequency changes when the sound enters the water, because the wave now travels faster.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know something must change when the medium changes, and frequency is the quantity they feel most comfortable adjusting. Seeing v and f side by side in v = f λ suggests they rise together.
misconceptions.correction: Frequency is set by the source, which is still vibrating at the same rate, so f stays the same and the pitch does not change. With f fixed, λ = v ÷ f, so the wavelength changes by exactly the same factor as the speed.

misconceptions.question: How should the wavelength of ripples in a ripple tank be measured?
misconceptions.correct: Measure the distance across about ten wavelengths on the frozen shadow pattern and divide by ten.
misconceptions.misconception: Just put a ruler between two neighbouring crests and read off the wavelength; measuring more than one is a waste of time.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The definition mentions one wavelength, so measuring one seems to be exactly what is asked. The size of the uncertainty relative to a 2 cm gap is not obvious to a student holding a millimetre rule.
misconceptions.correction: A single ripple shadow is a few centimetres across, blurred, and moving, so a millimetre-scale uncertainty is a large percentage of it. Measuring ten wavelengths and dividing by ten spreads that same uncertainty over ten times the distance.

misconceptions.question: What are the units of frequency and of wave speed?
misconceptions.correct: Frequency, f, in hertz, Hz; wave speed, v, in metres per second, m/s.
misconceptions.misconception: Frequency is measured in metres per second, because it says how much wave goes past you.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Frequency, wavelength and speed all appear in one equation and all describe motion, so their units get pooled. Metres per second is the unit students meet first and reach for by default.
misconceptions.correction: Hertz counts waves per second and carries no distance at all. Metres per second belongs to the wave speed. Getting the unit right is a check on which quantity is being calculated.

misconceptions.question: Is the amplitude the displacement of a point at any instant?
misconceptions.correct: The amplitude is the maximum displacement of a point away from its undisturbed position, not its displacement at an arbitrary moment.
misconceptions.misconception: The amplitude is just the displacement of a point on the wave — wherever the point happens to be.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Amplitude and displacement are defined in the same sentence and share a unit, so the word 'maximum' is dropped when the definition is recalled quickly.
misconceptions.correction: Displacement changes continuously between zero and a maximum as the point oscillates. The amplitude is that maximum value, reached only at a crest or a trough.

misconceptions.question: If the amplitude of a wave is increased, what happens to its frequency?
misconceptions.correct: Nothing: amplitude and frequency are independent, and the wave speed is unchanged too.
misconceptions.misconception: A bigger amplitude means a higher frequency, because a bigger wave carries more.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both quantities are described loosely as making the wave 'bigger' or 'stronger', and louder sounds do feel more energetic, so the two properties are merged into a single idea of intensity.
misconceptions.correction: Amplitude is a distance measured from the undisturbed position; frequency is a count of waves per second. Turning up the volume raises the amplitude of a note while its pitch, and therefore its frequency, is unchanged.

misconceptions.question: In the echo method, how is the distance the sound travels worked out?
misconceptions.correct: The sound travels to the wall and back, so the distance is twice the distance from the student to the wall.
misconceptions.misconception: The sound travels the distance from the student to the wall, so speed = distance to the wall ÷ echo time.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Only one distance is measured in the experiment, so that measurement is used directly. The return journey is invisible and easy to leave out of the calculation.
misconceptions.correction: The echo time covers the whole round trip. Speed = (2 × distance to the wall) ÷ time. Leaving out the factor of two halves the answer, giving about 170 m/s instead of about 340 m/s.

misconceptions.question: How is the wave equation rearranged to find a wavelength or a frequency?
misconceptions.correct: From v = f λ: λ = v ÷ f and f = v ÷ λ. The speed is always the quantity being divided.
misconceptions.misconception: You divide the two numbers you are given, whichever way round they come, or you multiply whenever the equation has a multiplication sign in it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember that the equation involves f and λ and reach for an operation before identifying which quantity is the unknown. The multiplication sign in the printed equation encourages multiplying in every case.
misconceptions.correction: Write down which quantity is missing first. Only when the wave speed is the unknown do you multiply; when frequency or wavelength is unknown, divide the speed by the quantity you have. A quick check of units confirms it: m/s ÷ Hz gives metres.

misconceptions.question: A wavelength is given in centimetres and a frequency in kilohertz. What must be done before using v = f λ?
misconceptions.correct: Convert to the units the equation uses: wavelength, λ, in metres, m, and frequency, f, in hertz, Hz.
misconceptions.misconception: The numbers can be put straight into the equation as they are given, because the equation works with any units.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The arithmetic still produces an answer, and nothing in the calculation flags the error. Data are printed in convenient units, which makes them look ready to use.
misconceptions.correction: Convert first: 2.4 cm is 0.024 m and 3 kHz is 3000 Hz. Using centimetres makes the speed a hundred times too large, which is why an answer should always be checked against a sensible value.

misconceptions.question: What exactly does the period of a wave measure?
misconceptions.correct: The period is the time taken for one complete wave to pass a point.
misconceptions.misconception: The period is the time the whole train of waves takes to go past you, from the first wave to the last.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In ordinary use a 'period' is a stretch of time with a beginning and an end, such as a lesson, so it is read as the duration of the whole event rather than of one repeat.
misconceptions.correction: The period is the time for one repeat only, so it is usually a fraction of a second. If eight waves pass in 2.0 s, the period is 0.25 s and the frequency is 4 Hz.

misconceptions.question: Does raising the frequency of a sound in air raise its speed?
misconceptions.correct: No: the wave speed is fixed by the medium, so a higher frequency gives a shorter wavelength instead.
misconceptions.misconception: Higher frequency means the waves are being made faster, so they must travel faster through the air.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The equation v = f λ shows v rising with f if the wavelength is assumed to stay put, and 'faster' is used loosely for both the rate of vibration and the speed of travel.
misconceptions.correction: In a given medium v is essentially constant, so f and λ vary inversely. If they did not, the high and low notes of a chord would reach a listener at different times.

misconceptions.question: How is the frequency of the ripples in a ripple tank found?
misconceptions.correct: Read it from the signal generator driving the dipper, since the ripples are produced at the frequency the dipper vibrates at.
misconceptions.misconception: Count the number of ripple crests you can see across the tank; that number is the frequency.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Counting crests is the only counting the apparatus obviously offers, and 'number of waves' in the definition of frequency is remembered without the words 'passing a point each second'.
misconceptions.correction: Frequency is a count per second at one point, not a count of crests across a picture. The number of crests visible depends on the size of the tank; the frequency is set by the dipper and read from the signal generator.

mcqs.stem: A transverse wave is drawn as a graph of displacement against distance, with the undisturbed position shown as a centre line. What is the amplitude of this wave?

options.text: The maximum displacement of a point on the wave from its undisturbed position
options.rationale: This is the specification definition: amplitude is measured from the undisturbed line to a crest or trough.

options.text: The vertical distance from the bottom of a trough to the top of the next crest
options.rationale: The most visible measurement on the diagram, but it is twice the amplitude.

options.text: The displacement of a point on the wave at the moment it is measured
options.rationale: Drops the word 'maximum'; displacement varies continuously as the point oscillates.

options.text: The distance a point on the wave travels while one whole wave passes
options.rationale: Confuses the size of the oscillation with the path length covered during one period.

mcqs.stem: A diagram shows several complete transverse waves. Which distance on the diagram is one wavelength?

options.text: From the top of one crest to the bottom of the trough immediately next to it
options.rationale: The two named features are adjacent, but this gap is only half a wavelength.

options.text: From the top of one crest to the top of the crest immediately next to it
options.rationale: Crest to adjacent crest is a point on one wave to the equivalent point on the adjacent wave.

options.text: From the undisturbed centre line up to the top of the crest above it
options.rationale: This is the amplitude, measured on the displacement axis rather than along the wave.

options.text: From the first crest on the diagram to the last crest on the diagram
options.rationale: Measures the whole wave train shown, rather than one repeat of the pattern.

mcqs.stem: On a displacement–distance diagram, crests occur at 4 cm, 12 cm and 20 cm along the axis. Each crest reaches 3 cm above the undisturbed line and each trough reaches 3 cm below it. What are the amplitude and the wavelength?

options.text: amplitude 6 cm, wavelength 8 cm
options.rationale: Correct wavelength, but the amplitude has been taken from trough to crest.

options.text: amplitude 3 cm, wavelength 4 cm
options.rationale: Correct amplitude, but crest-to-trough has been taken as the wavelength.

options.text: amplitude 3 cm, wavelength 8 cm
options.rationale: Amplitude is measured from the undisturbed line (3 cm) and the crests are 8 cm apart.

options.text: amplitude 6 cm, wavelength 4 cm
options.rationale: Both errors together: full height read as amplitude and half a wave read as the wavelength.

mcqs.stem: What does the frequency of a wave tell you?

options.text: The speed at which the waves travel through the material
options.rationale: 'Frequent' is read as 'fast'; this describes the wave speed instead.

options.text: The number of complete waves in each metre of the wave
options.rationale: Keeps the counting but attaches it to distance rather than to time.

options.text: The distance each point on the wave moves from rest
options.rationale: Describes the amplitude, the other quantity used to describe wave motion.

options.text: The number of complete waves that pass a point each second
options.rationale: This is the specification definition of frequency.

mcqs.stem: The dipper in a ripple tank produces 5 complete ripples every second. Which statement gives the frequency correctly?

options.text: The frequency is 5 hertz, written as 5 Hz
options.rationale: Five waves passing a point each second is a frequency of 5 Hz.

options.text: The frequency is 0.2 hertz, written as 0.2 Hz
options.rationale: Takes the reciprocal unnecessarily; 0.2 s is the period, not the frequency.

options.text: The frequency is 5 metres per second, or 5 m/s
options.rationale: Right number, but m/s is the unit of wave speed, not of frequency.

options.text: The frequency is 5 seconds, written as 5 s
options.rationale: Uses the unit of period, treating period and frequency as the same quantity.

mcqs.stem: A wave has a frequency of 40 Hz. What is its period?

options.rationale: The digits of 1 ÷ 40 with the decimal point misplaced by one position.
T = 1/f = 1 ÷ 40 = 0.025 s, in seconds as the specification requires.
The calculation is right but the answer is given in hertz; period, T, is in seconds, s.
Carries the frequency value straight across, treating period and frequency as equal.

mcqs.stem: A sound wave crosses a room at 340 m/s. What is travelling at 340 m/s?

options.text: Each particle of air, which is carried from the source to the listener
options.rationale: Assumes matter makes the journey; particles only oscillate about a fixed position.

options.text: The vibrating source, which produces 340 complete waves each second
options.rationale: Reads the figure as a count of waves per second, which would be a frequency.

options.text: The wave, and the energy it transfers, moving through the air
options.rationale: The wave speed is the speed at which the energy is transferred through the medium.

options.text: The gap between one compression and the next compression in the air
options.rationale: Names the wavelength, a distance, rather than a speed.

mcqs.stem: Which equation correctly links wave speed, frequency and wavelength?

options.text: wave speed = frequency ÷ wavelength
options.rationale: Right quantities, wrong operation, from remembering the letters but not the structure.

options.text: frequency = wave speed × wavelength
options.rationale: A rearrangement error: the speed, not the frequency, is the product of the other two.

options.text: wavelength = frequency × wave speed
options.rationale: Another wrong subject; multiplying gives the speed, never the wavelength.

options.text: wave speed = frequency × wavelength
options.rationale: The wave equation as the specification states it, v = f λ; all waves obey it.

mcqs.stem: A sound wave in air has a frequency of 170 Hz and a wavelength of 2.0 m. What is its wave speed?

options.rationale: v = f λ = 170 × 2.0 = 340 m/s, the expected speed of sound in air.

options.text: 85 m/s
options.rationale: From 170 ÷ 2.0; the two given quantities have been divided instead of multiplied.
From 2.0 ÷ 170; divided the other way round, giving an impossibly small speed.
Adds the two numbers, the fallback when the relationship is not recalled.

mcqs.stem: Ripples on a water surface travel at 0.24 m/s and have a frequency of 8.0 Hz. What is their wavelength?

options.rationale: From 0.24 × 8.0; multiplying regardless of which quantity is unknown.
λ = v ÷ f = 0.24 ÷ 8.0 = 0.030 m, a wavelength of 3.0 cm.
From 8.0 ÷ 0.24; the division has been done the wrong way round.
The right division with the decimal point misplaced by two positions.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the wave equation v = f λ is correct?

options.text: It applies only to transverse waves, such as ripples on water
options.rationale: Ties the equation to the crest-and-trough diagram used to introduce it.

options.text: It applies only while a wave stays inside one single material
options.rationale: The equation holds in both media; it is v and λ that take new values.

options.text: It applies to all waves, both transverse and longitudinal ones
options.rationale: The specification states that all waves obey the wave equation, sound included.

options.text: It applies only to waves that travel through a material medium
options.rationale: Would exclude light in a vacuum, which also obeys the wave equation.

mcqs.stem: (Physics only) A sound wave of frequency 500 Hz travels through air at 340 m/s and then passes into water, where sound travels at 1500 m/s. What happens as it enters the water?

options.text: The frequency increases and the wavelength stays the same
options.rationale: Assumes the faster speed must come from a higher frequency.

options.text: The frequency stays at 500 Hz and the wavelength decreases
options.rationale: Correct about frequency, but treats a faster wave as having shorter waves.

options.text: The frequency increases and the wavelength increases as well
options.rationale: Raises everything together, ignoring that the source fixes the frequency.

options.text: The frequency stays at 500 Hz and the wavelength increases
options.rationale: The source rate is unchanged, so with f fixed and v larger, λ = v ÷ f must increase.

mcqs.stem: (Physics only) A sound wave of frequency 500 Hz passes from air, where its speed is 340 m/s, into water, where its speed is 1500 m/s. What is its wavelength in the water?

options.rationale: λ = v ÷ f = 1500 ÷ 500 = 3.0 m, since the frequency is unchanged at 500 Hz.
Uses the speed in air, as though crossing the boundary changed nothing about v.
From 500 ÷ 1500; the division has been done the wrong way round.
From 1500 ÷ 340, dividing the two speeds instead of using the frequency.

mcqs.stem: Two microphones are placed 1.5 m apart in a straight line and connected to a fast timer, which records the interval between a sharp sound reaching one and then the other. How is the speed of sound obtained?

options.text: Multiply the distance between the microphones by the recorded time interval
options.rationale: Reaches for a multiplication without checking which quantity is unknown.

options.text: Divide the distance between the microphones by the recorded time interval
options.rationale: Speed = distance ÷ time, using the separation the sound covers between the signals.

options.text: Divide the recorded time interval by the distance between the two microphones
options.rationale: Right quantities in the wrong order; this gives seconds per metre.

options.text: Divide the distance between the microphones by twice the recorded interval
options.rationale: Imports the factor of two from the echo method, where the sound does travel twice.

mcqs.stem: A student stands 85 m from a large flat wall, claps once, and hears the echo 0.50 s later. What value does this give for the speed of sound in air?

options.rationale: From 85 ÷ 0.50, leaving out the return journey to the wall.
Doubles the distance and also halves the time, correcting for the echo twice over.
The sound covers 2 × 85 = 170 m in 0.50 s, so v = 170 ÷ 0.50 = 340 m/s.
From 85 × 0.50; multiplying the given values instead of dividing.

mcqs.stem: A strobe light freezes the shadow pattern of ripples on the paper below a ripple tank. Which measurement gives the wavelength most reliably?

options.text: Measure the gap between two neighbouring crests of the pattern with a rule
options.rationale: Matches the definition literally, but a 2 cm blurred gap carries a large uncertainty.

options.text: Measure from a crest of the pattern to the next trough and record that
options.rationale: Crest to adjacent trough is only half a wavelength.

options.text: Measure the height of a crest above the still water level and double it
options.rationale: Measures the size of the oscillation, which is an amplitude, not a wavelength.

options.text: Measure the distance across ten wavelengths of the pattern and divide it by ten
options.rationale: Spreading the millimetre-scale uncertainty over ten wavelengths reduces its effect.

mcqs.stem: In a ripple tank the signal generator drives the dipper at 12 Hz, and ten wavelengths of the frozen shadow pattern measure 24 cm. What is the speed of the ripples?

options.rationale: Takes 24 cm as one wavelength, forgetting to divide the ten-wavelength length by ten.

options.text: 29 m/s
options.rationale: Uses 2.4 cm in the equation without converting the wavelength to metres.
From 12 ÷ 0.024; divides when the unknown quantity is the speed.

mcqs.stem: In Required practical activity 8, a vibration generator driven by a signal generator sends waves along a stretched string, which settles into clear loops. How should the speed of the waves along the string be found?

options.text: Time how long one crest takes to travel the whole length of the string
options.rationale: Unsuitable apparatus: the pattern appears still and the transit is far too quick to time.

options.text: Read the frequency from the signal generator and multiply it by the wavelength
options.rationale: The wavelength is twice the length of one loop, and v = f λ gives the speed.

options.text: Read the frequency from the signal generator and divide it by the wavelength
options.rationale: Right measurements, wrong operation; dividing does not give a speed here.

options.text: Measure the amplitude of the vibrating string and multiply it by the frequency
options.rationale: Substitutes the height of the loops for the wavelength in the wave equation.

mcqs.stem: A buoy at sea moves up and down as waves pass it, completing one full up-and-down movement every 4.0 s. Which pair of values is correct?

options.text: period 4.0 s and frequency 4.0 Hz
options.rationale: Treats period and frequency as the same number in different units.

options.text: period 0.25 s and frequency 4.0 Hz
options.rationale: The two values have been swapped over between the quantities.

options.text: period 4.0 s and frequency 0.25 Hz
options.rationale: One complete wave takes 4.0 s, so T = 4.0 s and f = 1 ÷ 4.0 = 0.25 Hz.

options.text: period 4.0 Hz and frequency 0.25 s
options.rationale: The numbers are right but the units have been attached the wrong way round.

mcqs.stem: All sounds travel through air at about the same speed. Compared with a low-pitched note, a high-pitched note in the same room has

options.text: a greater speed, because more waves are being produced each second
options.rationale: Confuses the rate of vibration at the source with the speed of travel.

options.text: a longer wavelength, because more waves pass a point each second
options.rationale: Treats frequency and wavelength as rising together rather than inversely.

options.text: a larger amplitude, because a high note carries far more energy
options.rationale: Merges pitch and loudness into one idea of the wave being 'bigger'.

options.text: a shorter wavelength, because the speed of sound in air is fixed
options.rationale: With v fixed, λ = v ÷ f, so raising the frequency shortens the wavelength.

mcqs.stem: Which set of units must be used together in the equation v = f λ?

options.text: v in metres per second, f in hertz and λ in metres
options.rationale: Wave speed, v, in m/s; frequency, f, in Hz; wavelength, λ, in m, as specified.

options.text: v in metres per second, f in seconds and λ in metres
options.rationale: Gives frequency the unit of period, treating the two as interchangeable.

options.text: v in metres, f in hertz and λ in metres per second
options.rationale: Swaps the units of speed and wavelength, pooling the units of the equation.

options.text: v in metres per second, f in hertz and λ in centimetres
options.rationale: Keeps the unit the data are printed in instead of converting to metres.

mcqs.stem: What is meant by the period of a wave?

options.text: The time taken for the whole train of waves to pass a point
options.rationale: Reads 'period' as the duration of the whole event, as in everyday use.

options.text: The time taken for one complete wave to pass a point
options.rationale: The period is the time for a single repeat, calculated from T = 1/f.

options.text: The number of complete waves that pass a point in one second
options.rationale: Defines the frequency, the reciprocal quantity, instead of the period.

options.text: The time taken for the wave to travel one metre through air
options.rationale: Invents a time-per-distance quantity; the period is unrelated to any set distance.

mcqs.stem: A student wants the speed of ripples on the water surface in a ripple tank. Which method gives it?

options.text: Count the crests visible across the tank and multiply that by the wavelength
options.rationale: Counts crests in a picture rather than waves per second at one point.

options.text: Read the frequency from the signal generator and divide it by the wavelength
options.rationale: Uses the right two measurements but the wrong operation between them.

options.text: Read the frequency from the signal generator and multiply by the wavelength
options.rationale: The dipper sets the frequency and v = f λ then gives the speed of the ripples.

options.text: Measure the amplitude of the ripples and multiply that by their frequency
options.rationale: Puts the height of a ripple into the equation in place of the wavelength.
